title: The surah before sleep
hook: the Prophet ﷺ recited al-Mulk before sleeping, and it intercedes for its reader (Tirmidhi)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Asiya, and Asiya's prayer. Your line was a house near you. Did you pause at a door? Today a new surah begins, and it's one people keep by the bed. Day six hundred thirty-six.

What's the last thing you see before you sleep? For a lot of people it's a phone: one more video, one more scroll, the blue light on the ceiling. In many Muslim homes there's an older habit for the last minutes of the day. A short chapter, thirty verses, about five or ten minutes read aloud. Children learn it early. Grandparents say it from memory in the dark. It's surah sixty-seven, al-Mulk, the Sovereignty, and today we open the reason people read it at night.

It begins, in Pickthall's translation: "Blessed is He in Whose hand is the Sovereignty, and, He is Able to do all things." Al-mulk, the dominion, the kingship over everything. That first word, tabaraka, blessed, is why many people simply call the surah Tabarak. Now, two hadith in at-Tirmidhi's collection explain the bedtime habit. In one, a companion reports that the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ would not sleep until he had recited two surahs: as-Sajdah, and Tabarak, al-Mulk. In the other, the Prophet says that a surah of the Qur'an, thirty verses long, interceded for a man until he was forgiven, and he names it: Tabarak alladhi biyadihi al-mulk. Intercede means to speak up for someone, the way a friend might stand beside you in a hard meeting and say, I know this person. Here, in the hadith, it's a surah that does the speaking. Other narrations call al-Mulk a protector, and many Muslims understand it as a shield for its reader in the grave. Scholars discuss how strong each of these narrations is; the habit of reading it at night is very widely kept. And look at what the surah actually contains, because we'll spend three more days inside it. Death and life. The sky, looked at again and again. The earth made easy to walk on. Birds held up in the air. It's a surah about being held. That might be why it suits the moment a person lets go of the day and can't hold anything themselves.

The practice: read it before bed. For now, just the first verse. Sit, and say it, or hear it in your head: blessed is He in whose hand is the sovereignty. Notice your own hands. What have they been holding today? Let them rest open on your knees. Tonight, if you'd like, read all thirty verses before sleep, in Arabic or in any translation, slowly, phone face down. The bell holds the time.
Al-Mulk. The Sovereignty, surah sixty-seven, thirty verses the Prophet read before sleeping, which a hadith says interceded for its reader. Today's word.
Your line: it intercedes. Tonight, make the last thing you read a few verses of al-Mulk, or any words you'd want speaking up for you. Day six hundred thirty-six.

howItsDone: Many Muslims recite surah al-Mulk (also called Tabarak) every night before sleeping, following hadith that the Prophet did so and that this thirty-verse surah intercedes for its reader; children often learn it by heart.
